notes.why: Two eyes aimed up and out (39 degrees out and 33 up in the bont tick). The aperture mask could take a two-window shape; the outer parts would be invented.

Haller's organ reads radiant heat and carbon dioxide (Carr and Salgado 2019; Steullet and Guerin 1992). No phone input a web page can read stands in. The sheet recommends against painting warmth on skin colours; a body-detector spot is the closer stand-in and would be graded i.
Left unset on purpose: the plant's averaging would erase the passing shadow that ticks respond to.

rows: The Lone Star Tick and the dog ticks have one pair of eyes. The black-legged ticks have none.

In the tropical bont tick, of the Lone Star Tick’s genus, each eye has one lens and takes in a patch 43 degrees wide and 49 high, aimed 39 degrees out from straight ahead and 33 degrees up. The camera looks straight ahead, as you do.

A camel tick walks toward a dark disc on a pale background once the disc spans about 5 degrees, and toward the outline of a camel as small as a real one 18 metres away. The picture is blurred to match, and that reading is this app’s own.

The tropical bont tick is most sensitive to blue light near 480 nanometres, with a single peak. The picture is drawn in grey from the camera’s blue and green, and that rendering is this app’s invention.

The sheep tick, in the same genus as the black-legged ticks, has two rows of about twenty light-sensitive cells along its upper sides. In a laboratory, its nymphs did almost all their walking in the dark.

A questing tick grips a grass tip with its back two pairs of legs and holds the front pair out, ready to climb onto a passing host. Those front legs carry Haller’s organ, which smells and senses heat.

Lone Star Ticks steer by radiant heat through a covered pit on each front leg, and at least seven in ten adult females detected a square 10 centimetres across, heated to 40 degrees Celsius, from a metre away. An ordinary phone cannot sense that heat, so it is left out.

In the tropical bont tick, one receptor cell in that same organ responds most to changes in carbon dioxide of a hundredth of a percent around the level in open air. No phone records carbon dioxide, so it is left out.
Ticks also find hosts by body odour, moisture and vibration, and none of these reaches a camera.
